newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Europe-Asia bilateral forum lauds multilateralism.
newsitem.headline: Europe-Asia bilateral forum lauds multilateralism.

text.p: An economic forum dedicated to building bilateral ties between Europe and Asia ended with a consensus that multilateralism is the way to go.

"As important as intraregional links are, the ultimate goal is global integration and liberalization," said Mah Bow Tan, Singapore's Minister of Communications, at the close of the Europe/East Asia meeting of the World Economic Forum.
That theme was sounded throughout the three-day conference, which brought together economic policymakers and business people from Europe and Asia.

With the European Union on its way to monetary union, delegates dedicated much of the conference to studying ways Asian countries can work together to maintain stability in currency and other financial markets.

Ian McFarlane, governor of the Reserve Bank of Australia, charged that Asian nations do not have enough influence in international bodies such as the Bank for International Settlements and therefore should work together more closely.
Australia has been a vocal proponent of a BIS-type organization for Asia only.
Other Asian policymakers agreed on the need for close cooperation but stopped short of advocating an Asian BIS.
Indeed, Hong Kong's Financial Secretary Donald Tsang said that bilateral and regional commitments of the territory must take second place to its multilateral arrangements.

"We in Hong Kong have always believed in a multilateral system, so the BIS is the ideal place for dealing in issues of this kind," Tsang said in an interview with Reuters Financial Television during the conference.

Eisuke Sakakibara, director general at Japan's Ministry of Finance, said the U.S. also must take a role in stabilizing Asian markets in times of crisis because of the huge amount of dollar reserves held in the region.
While keen on regional and bilateral pacts to spur trade and investment, business leaders also trumpeted the importance of a global regime.

Christopher Roberts, Britain's deputy secretary of trade and industry, said that while European and Asian business people in the two regions share the same needs, convergence was a "global" phenomenon not limited to the two regions.

Victor Fung, chairman of the Hong Kong Trade Development Council, urged delegates not to view organizations such as APEC (Asia Pacific Economic Cooperation) and ASEM (Asia Europe Meeting) as thwarting global free trade.

"These organizations are all there to promote the further development of the multilateral world trade system and are not separate efforts that insulate and make smaller groupings that are actually protectionist in nature," he said.
APEC opened its fourth summit in Manila today.
